newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada telcos jump on new competition rules.
newsitem.headline: Canada telcos jump on new competition rules.

text.p: Shares of BCE Inc and other telephone utilities rose sharply on Friday as new rules allowing competition in Canada's local telephone market were seen as less negative for the phone companies than first expected, analysts said.
BCE shares were up 3.65 to 69.40 in Toronto on more than 2.2 million shares. TELUS Corp was up 2.05 to 22.10 on more than 900,000 shares.
BC Telecom Inc rallied 1.15 to 29.20 and Maritime Telegraph & Telephone Co was up 0.80 to 24.80.

On Thursday, the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) announced new rules ending the long-time monopoly in local telephone services held by the Stentor alliance of established phone companies.

Although the Stentor companies -- which includes Canada's biggest telephone concerns such as BCE's Bell Canada unit and BC Tel -- will have to open their local networks to alternative local exchange carriers such as AT&T and Sprint Corp, they will not be forced to rent them at wholesale rates.
"The market had probably priced in more negative expectations in the short run for the (Stentor) telephone companies. They avoided damage in this decision," said Doug Kirk, of Nesbitt Burns.
"Generally, people are pleased with the outcome of the decision. Everyone is very optimistic with what has been announced," said Imtiaz Khan of Research Capital Corp.
Kirk said BCE shares were also up because of improving prospects at its Northern Telecom Ltd unit. Nortel shares have rallied all week, while BCE shares were flat ahead of the CRTC decision.

The new rules will also allow "convergence" between Canada's telephone and cable television broadcast sectors, permitting phone companies to offer cable services and cable companies to get into the local telephone sector.
That would allow a melding of the C$8 billion local telephone and C$3 billion cable broadcasting markets.

While Canada's telco stocks rallied and its cable company operators such as Groupe Videotron Ltee and Rogers Communications Inc were cheering the CRTC decision, analyst Doug Cunningham at Midland Walwyn was more cautious about the CRTC decision.
Cunningham said there was no guarantee that the Stentor companies would get a proposed C$3-a-month increase in local rates on January 1. They will still have to argue their case before the CRTC.
"There has been a knee-jerk reaction because everyone sees a C$3 increase," Cunningham said.

Also, tough competitors like AT&T and Sprint, which have taken long-distance market share from Bell Canada and others, woulld not be that keen to enter unprofitable local service sectors, Cunningham said.
Instead, they will focus on profitable high-density urban residential markets and the lucrative business service sector.

"They are already doing business with corporate Canada. There will be the opportunity for these other carriers to cream-skim in apartment buildings and multiple-unit dwellings along the bus routes and subway lines," Cunningham said.

To counter that sort of intrusion, Bell Canada and other Stentor companies would likely ask the CRTC this year to allow then to reduce their basic service rates for business clients," Cunningham said.
"They will have to react, otherwise they will lose a lot of business," he said.
